strengths: Introduces SwissGov-RSD, the first naturalistic, document-level, cross-lingual dataset for token-level semantic difference recognition, filling a genuine gap since prior work (iSTS-RSD) relies on synthetic augmentation

Careful and transparent annotation methodology: detailed guidelines (Appendix A.2), a trial phase with feedback before the main phase, dual annotators per language pair with overlap-based validation, and multiple agreement metrics (IoU, F1, span-level label correlations)

Comprehensive and well-structured evaluation spanning unsupervised (DiffAlign), few-shot prompted LLMs (open and closed, including reasoning models), fine-tuned LLMs, and fine-tuned encoders, plus an LLM-based label-projection approach with manual quality checks (Appendix F)

Central claim — that performance on synthetic benchmarks does not transfer to naturalistic settings (drops of up to ~78 Spearman points) — is well supported by Table 3 and the ablations in Appendix H, with additional analyses of decoding failures (Table 4), positional effects (Figure 5), and annotator-discrepancy impact (Appendix A.4)

Good reproducibility: code and data (CC BY) released, model/training details and prompts provided, and inference-time comparison included; the paper honestly reports weak annotation agreement and its implications rather than hiding them
weaknesses: The dataset is modest in size (224 document pairs, ~180k tokens per pair set) and coverage: English-centric, closely related European languages, single domain (Swiss government), limiting generality of the conclusions

Annotator agreement is low in absolute terms (mean IoU 11–32, F1 18–55; very divergent span counts, especially EN-DE), and only two annotators per pair with 25 overlapping documents per language pair; system rankings could be unstable, as the authors themselves acknowledge via Sarti et al. (2025)

Several LLM fine-tuning experiments are missing for SwissGov-RSD ('-' entries) due to computational constraints, and the striking failure of fine-tuned GPT-4o-mini (from 81.6 on iSTS-RSD to 1.1–5.3) is not deeply diagnosed beyond speculation about overfitting to augmentation patterns

No train/test split for SwissGov-RSD is described (the whole dataset is used for evaluation), precluding in-domain fine-tuning experiments and creating future contamination risk; fine-tuned models are trained only on synthetic data

Evaluation relies on a single metric family (Spearman, with Kendall in appendix) on heavily skewed label distributions (90% equivalent tokens) and whitespace tokenization, with LLM outputs padded/truncated heuristically when lengths mismatch, which could distort correlation estimates
LLM-based label projection injects some noise into the projected training labels (34–46% of samples needed at least one edit in manual checks)

strengths: Novel and practically relevant resource: SwissGov-RSD is the first human-annotated, document-level, cross-lingual dataset for token-level semantic difference recognition, built from naturally occurring differences in Swiss government texts rather than synthetic augmentation. This fills a genuine gap relative to iSTS-RSD.

Transparent and reasonably rigorous annotation methodology: written guidelines (full guidelines in appendix), a trial phase with feedback, 25 overlapping documents per language pair for validation, and honest reporting of modest span-level agreement (IoU/F1) with a qualitative analysis of annotator strategies (Appendix A.4). The comparison to Kocmi et al. (2024) on error-span annotation agreement provides useful context.

Broad and well-structured evaluation: 12 unsupervised encoder configurations, 6 LLMs (open/closed, reasoning variants), few-shot prompting, fine-tuning (LoRA and OpenAI fine-tuning), and an LLM-based label projection pipeline with a manual post-edit validation (Appendix F). Results are reported on both the new benchmark and iSTS-RSD, plus Kendall tau-b, position-based analysis, and inference-time comparison.

Clear and credible central finding: performance collapses from iSTS-RSD to SwissGov-RSD (e.g., fine-tuned GPT-4o-mini drops from ~80 to ~1-5 Spearman), supporting the claim that synthetically augmented benchmarks overestimate real-world capability. The failure-mode analysis (format errors, underlabeling, length sensitivity) adds useful insight.
Good reproducibility posture: code and data released with license handling (CC BY for labels), detailed hyperparameters, prompts, dataset statistics, and model descriptions in appendices.
Limitations are candidly discussed (language/script coverage, two-annotator setup, prompting simplicity).
weaknesses: Annotation reliability is weak, especially for EN-DE: span-level agreement is low (mean IoU 10-11, F1 ~18 for EN-DE) and the two annotators diverge substantially in the number of annotated differences. While framed as within normal ranges, this noise directly caps achievable correlations and makes the very low absolute system scores on SwissGov-RSD hard to interpret; the paper does not quantify how much of the model-benchmark gap may be attributable to label noise versus genuine model failure.

The dataset-construction decision to merge annotations by manually selecting whichever annotator 'adheres more to the guidelines' is subjective and not fully specified; with only two annotators per language pair, systematic annotator bias could propagate into the gold labels.

An important experimental gap: no system is ever fine-tuned on SwissGov-RSD data itself (even a small in-domain or few-shot-tuning ablation on a held-in portion). Consequently, the conclusion 'synthetic training data does not transfer' is demonstrated, but the arguably more actionable question—how much in-domain data is needed, or whether in-domain fine-tuning closes the gap—is left unaddressed, weakening the practical impact of the findings.

Asymmetric LLM evaluation: DeepSeek-R1 and o3-mini receive no SwissGov results with only a vague 'computational restraints' justification, and only the best iSTS-RSD performers were run on SwissGov, introducing selection effects in the cross-benchmark comparison.

Size and scope are modest: 224 documents per language pair from a small set of subdomains (Table 5 shows heavy skew, e.g., 86 documents from bfe.admin.ch), all English-centric and Latin-script, with no train/test split of the new data.

Several presentational/consistency errors that suggest incomplete proofreading: Table 10 lists implausible parameter counts (LaBSE '500B', gte-multilingual '685B'); Table 15 refers to 'Llama-3.2 8B' while the paper evaluates Llama-3.1 8B; a cross-reference to 'Appendix 13' is incorrect; the EN-IT iSTS extension and PAWS translation pipeline are described only in footnotes without quality analysis of the machine-translated evaluation data.

The task setup requires LLMs to emit per-token JSON over documents up to ~2800 words, a format that heavily disadvantages LLMs by design (Table 4 shows 7%+ decode failures); alternative output formats or structured-decoding approaches are not explored, so the claim 'LLMs are highly limited on this task' conflates task difficulty with output-format burden to some degree.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine gap: existing RSD/semantic-similarity resources are sentence-level, monolingual, or synthetic, and SwissGov-RSD is the first naturalistic, document-level, cross-lingual dataset with token-level difference annotations. The practical motivation (unnoticed discrepancies on multilingual government websites) is well supported by the Figure 1 example.

The annotation methodology is unusually thorough and transparent: detailed written guidelines, a trial phase with feedback before the main phase, an overlap of 25 document pairs per language pair for validation, agreement metrics (IoU, F1, Spearman correlation on fuzzy/exact span matches), and fair compensation. The full guidelines and interface instructions are in the appendix.

Agreement results are reported honestly rather than glossed over, including the low EN-DE span agreement, and the paper situates its overlap numbers relative to prior work on error-span annotation (Kocmi et al., 2024; Sarti et al., 2025). Appendix A.4 analyzes how annotator discrepancies affect system rankings and shows the main conclusion holds for both annotators.

The evaluation is broad and current: an unsupervised baseline (DiffAlign) with many encoder variants (including long-context encoders like ModernBERT, EuroBERT, MmBERT, bge-m3, Qwen3-Embedding), few-shot and fine-tuned LLMs (open and closed, with and without reasoning), and LLM-based label projection with a manual quality check of the projections (Appendix F).

The central empirical finding is clear and consequential: all systems show large drops from iSTS-RSD to SwissGov-RSD (e.g., fine-tuned GPT-4o-mini from ~80 to ~1-5 Spearman), and the paper provides useful secondary analyses (LLM decoding failures in Table 4, underlabeling near document ends, position-wise degradation in Figure 5, inference-time comparison in Appendix J).

Reproducibility is strong: code and data are released, prompts and fine-tuning details are given, licenses and model details are documented, and Kendall tau-b results are provided as a robustness check for Spearman ties.
weaknesses: The dataset is small: 224 multi-parallel documents (with only ~10-17% of tokens labeled as different), and it is used purely as a test set with no train/validation split. This limits its utility as a standalone benchmark for training and makes system comparisons on it statistically fragile, particularly given the modest annotator agreement (mean IoU as low as ~10-11 for EN-DE).

The headline claim that 'synthetically augmented datasets do not sufficiently reflect realistic scenarios' is confounded: SwissGov-RSD differs from iSTS-RSD simultaneously in domain (government vs. news/image descriptions), length (documents of hundreds of tokens), annotation provenance, and label distribution. The paper acknowledges this but does not disentangle the factors, so the drop cannot be attributed specifically to synthetic vs. naturalistic data.

Coverage of LLMs on SwissGov-RSD is incomplete: several LLMs (Llama-8B, GPT-4o-mini few-shot, DeepSeek-R1, o3-mini) were simply not evaluated on the new dataset 'due to computational restraints', so the LLM conclusions rest on a small subset, and the reasoning models are tested only at low reasoning effort.

Only two annotators per language pair with overlap on 25 of 224 documents; the merged annotations involve subjective adjudication ('we include the annotations adhering more to the guidelines'), which could introduce bias toward the authors' own interpretation of the guidelines and is not independently validated.

The evaluation relies heavily on token-level Spearman correlation over a highly skewed ordinal label distribution; while Kendall tau-b is reported in the appendix, the main metric's sensitivity to the label distribution and tie structure is not deeply analyzed, and no significance testing or variance estimates are provided for system comparisons.

Scope limitations are real: English-centric pairs, three closely related European languages, a single (government) domain, and no non-Latin scripts, which the authors themselves note in the Limitations section.

Minor presentation issues: a table reference to 'Appendix 13' appears to be an error, some tables in the appendix have inconsistent naming (iSTS-RSD vs. RSD-iSTS), and the number of overlapping-token statistics in Table 2 (e.g., very different span counts between annotators for EN-DE) suggests the merged gold standard is noisy in ways not fully quantified.

strengths: The paper introduces SwissGov-RSD, the first naturalistic, document-level, cross-lingual dataset with human token-level semantic-difference annotations in three language pairs (EN-DE, EN-FR, EN-IT), addressing a genuine gap left by the synthetic iSTS-RSD benchmark.

The annotation effort is well documented and reasonably rigorous: written guidelines (Appendix A.2), a dedicated annotation interface, a trial phase with feedback, overlap-based validation with IoU/F1 and Spearman agreement, manual inspection of double-annotated and flagged documents, and an explicit analysis of how annotator discrepancies affect model evaluation (Appendix A.4).

The evaluation is broad and informative: 12 unsupervised encoder baselines, 6 LLMs (open/closed, reasoning models), few-shot prompting, LoRA/API fine-tuning, and a practical LLM-based label-projection method for cross-lingual fine-tuning, with a manual validation of the projected labels (Table 9).

The central finding -- a large performance drop from the synthetic iSTS-RSD to the naturalistic SwissGov-RSD (e.g., fine-tuned GPT-4o-mini: ~80 to ~4 Spearman) -- is clearly supported and interesting; the analysis of long-document behavior by token position and LLM output-format failures adds value.

Reproducibility is strong: code and data released under a stated license, detailed hyperparameters, full per-language and per-augmentation results in appendices, Kendall tau-b robustness checks, model licensing table, and inference-time comparison.
weaknesses: Dataset scale is modest: only 224 document pairs, with annotation validation on just 25 overlapping pairs per language pair; final documents carry only a single annotation, and inter-annotator Spearman agreement (43.6-65.1) is moderate, so the reliability ceiling for model scores is unclear.

There is no train/dev/test split for SwissGov-RSD and no in-domain fine-tuning experiment; all fine-tuning is on iSTS-RSD data, so the paper cannot cleanly separate 'the task is intrinsically hard on realistic data' from 'out-of-domain transfer fails'. A small in-domain training experiment would substantially strengthen the claims.

Several LLM cells in the main SwissGov results (Table 3) are missing 'due to computational restraints', which weakens the completeness of the LLM comparison and makes some cross-category statements rely on partial coverage.

The dataset is confined to one domain (Swiss government texts), English-centric, and limited to closely related Latin-script languages; the paper acknowledges this but it limits the generality of conclusions about cross-lingual RSD.

The low absolute model scores on SwissGov-RSD (often near zero, some negative) are interpreted as a generalization gap, but given moderate human agreement, some of this may reflect label noise or annotation-strategy variance; the authors partially address this (Appendix A.4) but a more definitive link between agreement levels and the interpretation of near-zero model performance is missing.
EN-IT trial-phase label agreement was quite low (correlations 27-41, Table 6) and does not appear to have triggered re-annotation or guideline revision comparable to the EN-DE annotator replacement.

Minor: text still contains typos ('annoted', 'Annotate a pair of' placeholder), and the manual merging/selection of annotations between annotators is a subjective step that is described but not quantified.

strengths: The paper introduces the first naturalistic, document-level, cross-lingual dataset for token-level semantic difference recognition (SwissGov-RSD), filling a genuine gap left by the synthetic iSTS-RSD benchmark (Vamvas and Sennrich, 2023). The motivation — real multilingual government content drifting across language versions — is concrete and practical.

The annotation methodology is transparent and reasonably rigorous: published guidelines (Appendix A.2), a custom annotation interface, a trial phase with feedback, paid annotators, and a thorough agreement analysis (IoU, F1, and Spearman correlation on fuzzy- and exact-matched spans, Table 2) that honestly reports moderate inter-annotator agreement (43.61–65.09) and contextualizes it against comparable span-annotation tasks.

The benchmarking effort is broad and current: unsupervised DiffAlign variants over many modern multilingual encoders (XLM-R+SimCSE, LaBSE, EuroBERT, MmBERT, bge-m3, Qwen3-Embedding), few-shot prompted LLMs (Llama-3.1 8B/405B, GPT-4o-mini/4o, DeepSeek-R1, o3-mini), fine-tuned LLMs, and fine-tuned encoders with an LLM-based label projection scheme that is itself manually validated (Appendix F).

The central empirical claim — that systems performing well on the synthetic iSTS-RSD collapse on naturalistic data (e.g., fine-tuned GPT-4o-mini: 81.6 → 3.9 Spearman on EN-DE) — is clearly demonstrated, and the appendix analyses (Kendall τ-b, per-annotator breakdowns in Table 7, token-position analysis in Figure 5, inference-time comparison) strengthen the robustness of the finding.

Good reproducibility posture: code and data released under clear licensing (CC BY labels, government text copyright documented), full prompts, fine-tuning hyperparameters, model inventories, and data statistics provided in appendices.
weaknesses: Dataset scale is modest: only 224 document pairs (roughly 170–196k tokens per language pair) from seven Swiss federal subdomains, and it is evaluated as a single monolithic test set with no train/dev/test split, limiting its use as a benchmark for training or leaderboard-style comparison.

Inter-annotator agreement is low-to-moderate and validation coverage is thin: only 25 overlapping documents per language pair, with token-level Spearman correlations of 43–65. Since best models score 5–25 on SwissGov-RSD, it is unclear how much of the observed 'gap' reflects genuine model failure versus noise in noisy gold labels; no significance testing or confidence intervals are reported anywhere.

The gold-label merging procedure (manually choosing between conflicting annotator annotations based on 'adherence to guidelines') is subjective and introduces researcher degrees of freedom that are not audited.

The dataset is English-centric, limited to closely related Latin-script languages and a single domain (government text); the paper acknowledges this, but it constrains the breadth of the claimed generalization findings.

Some experimental asymmetries weaken conclusions: fine-tuned LLM experiments are restricted to two models, several LLM results on SwissGov are omitted due to 'computational restraints', and English-side-only annotations in the iSTS-RSD cross-lingual test sets complicate direct comparison with the fully two-sided SwissGov annotations.

Presentation issues remain (e.g., 'human-annoted' typos, a dangling reference to 'Appendix 13', Figure 3 legend/placement), and the Skewed label distribution (10–17% differing tokens) is discussed but its impact on Spearman-based evaluation is not analyzed beyond a brief tie-robustness note.

The contribution is primarily a resource plus a negative result; there is little methodological novelty, so main-conference impact hinges on the dataset's scale and reliability, which are the weakest dimensions.

strengths: Introduces SwissGov-RSD, the first naturalistic, document-level, cross-lingual dataset for token-level semantic difference recognition (224 multi-parallel doc pairs in EN-DE, EN-FR, EN-IT), filling a clear gap left by the synthetic iSTS-RSD benchmark.

The annotation process is unusually well documented and carefully executed: written guidelines (full guidelines in appendix), a trial phase with feedback, two annotators per language pair, dedicated annotation tooling, fair compensation, and a multi-faceted agreement analysis (IoU, F1, fuzzy/exact span matching, token-level Spearman, Kendall's tau).

The evaluation is broad and current: unsupervised DiffAlign baselines with a dozen encoders (including long-context models like EuroBERT, Qwen3-Embedding, bge-m3), few-shot and fine-tuned LLMs (Llama-3.1, GPT-4o, DeepSeek-R1, o3-mini), plus an LLM-based label projection approach with a manual quality check of the projections (Appendix F).

The central finding — a large, consistent performance drop when moving from synthetic iSTS-RSD to the naturalistic dataset, with unsupervised encoders being unexpectedly robust and LLMs deteriorating sharply — is clearly supported by Table 3/11/12 and the supplementary position and length analyses (Figures 4-5, Table 4).

Strong reproducibility: code and data released under clear licensing (CC BY for labels), model details and hyperparameters specified, prompts and guidelines included in appendices, and limitations (language coverage, two-annotator setup, simple prompting) are candidly discussed.

Useful secondary analyses: per-annotator result breakdown (A.4) showing conclusions hold for both annotators, Kendall tau robustness check, inference-time comparison, and an Italian extension of iSTS-RSD enabling direct comparison.
weaknesses: Inter-annotator agreement is modest: token-level Spearman of 43.6-65.1 across language pairs and mean IoU of only ~24-44, with highly divergent span counts between annotators (e.g., 348 vs. 139 spans for EN-DE). While comparable to related span-annotation tasks, this noise floor complicates interpretation of very low model correlations, some of which are near zero or negative (Table 7).

The dataset is small (224 documents, ~173k-196k tokens per pair, only 25 overlapping documents for agreement validation), and the manual merging of overlapping annotations ('include the annotations adhering more to the guidelines') is a subjective curation step that is only briefly described.

The core 'synthetic-to-real gap' conclusion is somewhat confounded: all fine-tuned models are trained exclusively on synthetic iSTS-RSD data and there is no in-domain fine-tuning experiment on SwissGov-RSD (the dataset has no train/dev/test split). The gap therefore mixes distribution shift with out-of-domain effects; a small in-domain fine-tuning study would substantially strengthen the claim that data augmentation fails to imitate real-world scenarios.

LLM coverage on SwissGov-RSD is uneven due to 'computational restraints' (many dashes in Table 3), so some cross-model comparisons on the new benchmark are incomplete, and it is not fully clear how the 'best-performing on iSTS-RSD' selection was frozen without leaking the new benchmark's model selection.

Severe label imbalance (only 10-17% of tokens labeled as different, and 0-labeled tokens dominating the correlation computation) makes token-level Spearman scores difficult to interpret as a measure of practical utility; alternative metrics or sub-analyses restricted to difference spans would be informative.

Minor issues: typos ('human-annoted', 'iSTS-RSD' vs. 'RSD-iSTS' naming), the Italian iSTS-RSD extension is machine-translated (acknowledged), and some footnoted URLs/statements (e.g., dataset links) are placeholders that should be verified in the final version.
